# carry

Produce the present account and commitment interface for the next complete template invocation. The material may support a revision, an unresolved problem, or retaining something. Preserve the grounds needed for whatever uptake you propose.

## Original problem (task)
[d31d61f36df18c74] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input response (p.carry.0)

BODY
After weighing the three contributions, I see merit in combining elements rather than adopting any single proposal wholesale. The original account correctly spotlights the lack of a shared, durable reference (a written schedule) as a source of confusion, but the objection reminds me that the problem may also involve deeper relational dynamics that a mere spreadsheet cannot fix. The rival’s chore‑wheel idea offers a concrete, visual protocol that reduces reliance on memory and verbal agreements, and its log‑sheet component directly addresses the objection’s concern about a traceable record of exceptions. 

Thus, I propose a hybrid approach: (1) start with a brief, low‑stakes diagnostic talk to surface any underlying tensions or power imbalances; (2) agree on a visual chore‑wheel (paper or digital) that rotates weekly, complemented by a simple log of any swaps or deviations; (3) establish clear, enforceable ground‑rules for conflict resolution, including a short pause‑and‑share step and a defined consequence for repeated non‑compliance (e.g., temporary reassignment of the offending chore); (4) set a recurring 5‑minute check‑in (in‑person or via the shared board) to update availability and adjust the wheel; and (5) embed a feedback loop – a brief weekly satisfaction rating – to evaluate whether the system improves fairness and communication.  This blended model respects the need for an explicit coordination tool, acknowledges possible relational issues, and provides measurable ways to iterate.

I will leave the precise format of the wheel (paper vs. app) open pending the flatmates' technical comfort, and I will keep the evaluation criteria flexible so they can be refined after a trial month.
COMMITMENTS
1. Facilitate a short, neutral diagnostic conversation with all three flatmates to identify any relational or power‑dynamic factors beyond chore logistics. 2. Co‑design a visual chore‑wheel (printed poster or shared digital board) that assigns weekly responsibilities and includes a simple log for swaps, ensuring every roommate is comfortable with the chosen medium. 3. Draft a concise ground‑rules sheet that outlines the pause‑and‑share dispute process, specifies a concrete consequence for repeated breaches, and defines how chores will be rotated to maintain equity. 4. Schedule a 5‑minute weekly check‑in (or asynchronous update via the board) to capture schedule changes and adjust the wheel accordingly. 5. Implement a weekly satisfaction check (e.g., 1‑5 rating) and a brief review after the first month to assess the system’s effectiveness and decide on any adjustments.

COMMITMENTS
To act on these ideas, the flat would need to (1) schedule a short, neutral meeting where all three agree to try a written chore system; (2) choose a simple tool (a spreadsheet, a phone app, or a printed calendar) to list chores, assign them, and note each person’s availability; (3) set a recurring weekly or bi‑weekly check‑in (5‑10 minutes) to adjust the schedule as work hours change; (4) create a brief ‘ground‑rules’ sheet for handling disagreements (e.g., use ‘I’ statements, avoid blame, propose a compromise, and, if needed, rotate the disputed chore for a week); and (5) optionally reach out to the avoiding flatmate in a non‑confrontational way (perhaps via message) to ask if there’s a preferred communication mode or any personal stress they’d like to share, showing willingness to accommodate their comfort level. Implementing these steps would require each person’s commitment of a few minutes per week and a willingness to trial the new system for at least a month before evaluating its effectiveness.
